model_note.S:
cc: Recurrent one-sided headache with light sensitivity

HPI: 26 yo f. Patient reports: This episode began gradually 6 hours ago. It is on the left side of my head. It does not spread down my neck. It is throbbing. It is 7/10. Similar attacks last 12–24 hours, about twice a month. It began after I missed lunch and slept poorly. A dark quiet room helps. Light, sound and walking worsen it. Acetaminophen 500 mg helped a little. I have had the same pattern since age 19. It is the same left-sided throbbing pattern as before. Light hurts my eyes. I feel nauseated.

Patient perspective: Do I need a brain scan every time this happens?

PMH: Previously diagnosed migraine; no malignancy or immunosuppression.

PSH: No surgeries or hospitalizations.

Meds: Acetaminophen on 2–3 days per month; no daily medication.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink monthly. No recreational drugs. Medical student; lives with husband; regular periods, last period 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected.

FH: Mother has migraine; father hypertension; brother healthy.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports headache. Reports photophobia. Denies focal weakness. Denies thunderclap. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Prefers dim light, not toxic appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive; extraocular movements intact.

Neuro: Face symmetric; tongue midline; speech clear. Strength 5/5 in arms and legs bilaterally. Light touch symmetric in arms and legs. Neck flexion is comfortable without stiffness.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Review headache red flags, neurologic findings and pregnancy/medication contraindications; offer an individualized acute migraine treatment plan with clinician review and discuss nausea management; use a headache diary, regular meals and sleep, with follow-up in 2–4 weeks; explain emergency evaluation for a new sudden maximal headache, fever with stiff neck or focal deficit.

2. Assess fever, meningismus and systemic risk; urgent emergency evaluation and appropriate testing if infection is suspected; explain that the current absence of these features reduces but does not independently eliminate concern. If infection becomes a clinical concern, obtain blood cultures and consider lumbar puncture through the emergency team after safety assessment; testing must not delay urgent treatment.

3. Quantify every acute-medication day per month; counsel on avoiding escalation and arrange review if headache frequency or medication use increases; do not diagnose medication overuse from occasional use alone. Keep a headache and medication-day diary and arrange primary-care follow-up to review it in 4 weeks; refer to neurology if headaches become frequent or disabling despite initial management.

model_note.S:
cc: Recurrent one-sided headache with light sensitivity

HPI: 26 yo f. Patient reports: This episode began gradually 10 hours ago. It is on the left side of my head. It does not spread down my neck. It is throbbing. It is 7/10. Similar attacks last 12–24 hours, about twice a month. It began after I missed lunch and slept poorly. A dark quiet room helps. Light, sound and walking worsen it. Acetaminophen 500 mg helped a little. I have had the same pattern since age 19. It is the same left-sided throbbing pattern as before. Light hurts my eyes. I feel nauseated.

Patient perspective: Do I need a brain scan every time this happens?

PMH: Previously diagnosed migraine; no malignancy or immunosuppression.

PSH: No surgeries or hospitalizations.

Meds: Acetaminophen on 2–3 days per month; no daily medication.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink monthly. No recreational drugs. Medical student; lives with husband; regular periods, last period 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected.

FH: Mother has migraine; father hypertension; brother healthy.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports headache. Reports photophobia. Denies focal weakness. Denies thunderclap. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Prefers dim light, not toxic appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive; extraocular movements intact.

Neuro: Face symmetric; tongue midline; speech clear. Strength 5/5 in arms and legs bilaterally. Light touch symmetric in arms and legs. Neck flexion is comfortable without stiffness.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Review headache red flags, neurologic findings and pregnancy/medication contraindications; offer an individualized acute migraine treatment plan with clinician review and discuss nausea management; use a headache diary, regular meals and sleep, with follow-up in 2–4 weeks; explain emergency evaluation for a new sudden maximal headache, fever with stiff neck or focal deficit.

2. Assess fever, meningismus and systemic risk; urgent emergency evaluation and appropriate testing if infection is suspected; explain that the current absence of these features reduces but does not independently eliminate concern. If infection becomes a clinical concern, obtain blood cultures and consider lumbar puncture through the emergency team after safety assessment; testing must not delay urgent treatment.

3. Quantify every acute-medication day per month; counsel on avoiding escalation and arrange review if headache frequency or medication use increases; do not diagnose medication overuse from occasional use alone. Keep a headache and medication-day diary and arrange primary-care follow-up to review it in 4 weeks; refer to neurology if headaches become frequent or disabling despite initial management.
